title: Ilkhanate
capsule: The Ilkhanate was the Mongol successor state in Iran and the Middle East, founded by Hülegü Khan — grandson of Genghis Khan — following his campaigns of 1256–1260 that destroyed the Nizari Ismaili strongholds and sacked Baghdad in February 1258, killing the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim and ending the Abbasid Caliphate. The state reached its administrative peak under Ghazan Khan (r. 1295–1304), who converted to Islam in 1295, reformed taxation and coinage, and patronized Rashid al-Din's Compendium of Chronicles (Jami' al-Tawarikh). Abu Sa'id (r. 1316–1335) died without an heir in 1335, triggering the rapid dissolution of the Ilkhanate into competing successor dynasties — the Jalayirids, Chobanids, Muzaffarids, and Injuids — which divided its territories by the early 1340s.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core Ilkhanate territory (Iran, Iraq, Anatolia, Caucasus) is well documented through Persian administrative records, Rashid al-Din's chronicles, and numismatic evidence. Frontier zones in eastern Anatolia and the steppe border with the Golden Horde are less precisely defined; overall moderate to high confidence for the Iranian heartland.
